stances.claim: Under the Sereno dictum (Republic v. Sereno, May 11, 2018), quo warranto applies only when the act or omission was committed 'prior to or at the time of the appointment or election' relating to qualifications to hold office, rendering it invalid from the outset -- acts during incumbency cannot be QW subjects. The same principle applies to franchises: defects must pre-exist or be simultaneous with the grant, not arise from post-grant conduct.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-precedent transposition from public-office QW (Sereno) to franchise QW (ABS-CBN)

stances.claim: The acts and omissions alleged against ABS-CBN (the KBO pay-per-view operations, the PDR issuances, the corporate layering, the alleged failure to list in the PSE) were committed after the franchises were validly granted by law -- therefore, under the Sereno dictum, they cannot be the subjects of quo warranto. CJ maintains his prior view that impeachment (not QW) is the proper remedy for impeachable officials, but agrees with the pre-existing-invalidity principle.
stances.rhetorical_move: factual-temporal classification of the alleged acts against the doctrinal pre-existing-invalidity test

stances.claim: Under Gio-Samar v. DOTC (March 12, 2019), when a question before the SC involves a factual determination indispensable to resolving the legal issue, the Court will refuse to resolve the question regardless of allegations of compelling reasons -- so at the very least, the petitions should be remanded to the Court of Appeals to determine the factual questions before the SC can act on the legal issues.
stances.rhetorical_move: fact-finding-precedence doctrine to argue for remand even before doctrinal disposition

stances.claim: The Philippine Deposit Receipts at issue did not violate the constitutional 100% Filipino ownership/management requirement for mass media because PDRs do not grant ownership or management rights to foreigners -- they confer (a) the right to receive dividends of the underlying shares (less administrative expenses) and (b) the right to convert into shares of stock only if the converter is Filipino. The 100% Filipino-owned company that owns the underlying shares unqualifiedly controls and votes them.
stances.rhetorical_move: instrument-by-instrument rights-analysis to defeat the constitutional claim

stances.claim: Complaints about alleged franchise violations should be filed with the agencies that have regulatory jurisdiction (NTC, SEC), whose decisions are appealable to the CA and then to the SC. Even if violations are duly proven, the penalty under existing law is not forfeiture of the franchise but a fine, a refund of fees paid, and/or a halt to the service complained of.
stances.rhetorical_move: remedy-proportionality argument paired with jurisdictional channeling

stances.claim: At bottom, the fate of ABS-CBN and ABS-CBN Convergence rests with Congress (which may approve, veto, or allow the franchise bill to lapse into law) and the President -- not with the Supreme Court. The QW petitions are doctrinally untenable; the proper political-branch route is the franchise legislation itself.
stances.rhetorical_move: branch-allocation closing -- separating doctrinal review from policy outcome

notable_anecdotes: CJ's teacher-of-law aside -- 'Since my days as a professor of law up to now, I have never believed in spoon-feeding. In my humble opinion, the best way to learn is to think solutions for ourselves in given scenarios' -- converting a column into a Socratic classroom and modeling pedagogical philosophy in a constitutional-law dispute.

The reservation-and-agreement structure on Sereno: 'I maintain my opinion published a year ago that impeachment, not QW, is the proper remedy to remove impeachable officials like Supreme Court (SC) justices. But I agree with the dictum that for QW to apply, the invalidity must be pre-existing.' -- a textbook example of CJ separating his disagreement with a holding from his agreement with one of its doctrinal premises.

The full-text quotation of the Sereno dictum -- 'act or omission was committed prior to or at the time of the appointment or election relating to an official's qualifications to hold office as to render such appointment or election invalid... Acts or omissions... committed during the incumbency of a validly appointed and/or validly elected official cannot be the subject of a quo warranto proceeding...' -- providing the doctrinal hinge of the column.

The institutional-channel closing: the proper venues for franchise-violation complaints are the NTC and SEC, appealable to the CA and SC, with penalties limited to fines, refunds, or service halts -- and the franchise's actual fate lies with Congress (which may approve, veto, or allow the bill to lapse) and the President -- a clear separation-of-powers map for a politically charged dispute.

one_paragraph_summary: In this Part 2 column, Panganiban delivers his 'modest answers' to the questions he posed last Sunday on Solicitor General Jose C. Calida's quo warranto petitions against ABS-CBN and ABS-CBN Convergence. Opening with a pedagogical aside that he has never believed in spoon-feeding, he turns to doctrine: under Republic v. Sereno (May 11, 2018), quo warranto applies only when the act or omission was 'prior to or at the time of the appointment or election' rendering the holding invalid from the outset -- acts during incumbency cannot be QW subjects. Sereno was ousted precisely because her pre-appointment failure to file some SALNs negated the constitutional integrity qualification, which is how Teresita J. Leonardo-De Castro became the de jure 'First Female and 24th Chief Justice.' CJ maintains his prior view that impeachment, not QW, is the proper remedy for impeachable officials, but agrees with the pre-existing-invalidity premise. The same logic applies to franchises: the defects must pre-exist the grant. ABS-CBN's alleged KBO operations, PDR issuances, corporate layering, and alleged PSE non-listing all post-date the validly enacted franchises, so under the Sereno dictum, they cannot be QW subjects. He invokes Gio-Samar v. DOTC (March 12, 2019), where the SC held that when factual issues are indispensable to legal issues, the Court will refuse to resolve them regardless of allegations of compelling reasons -- meaning at minimum the petitions should be remanded to the Court of Appeals for factual determination before the SC can act. On the merits of the PDR question, he argues the instruments did not violate the constitutional 100% Filipino ownership/management requirement for mass media: PDRs grant only the right to receive dividends (less administrative expenses) and the right to convert into shares of stock if the converter is Filipino, while a 100% Filipino-owned company unqualifiedly controls and votes the underlying shares. Complaints about alleged violations belong with the NTC and SEC (appealable to the CA and SC), and the penalties under existing law are fines, refunds of fees paid, or halts of the service complained of -- not franchise forfeiture. He closes by allocating institutional responsibility: at bottom, the fate of ABS-CBN and ABS-CBN Convergence rests with Congress (which may approve, veto, or allow the franchise bill to lapse) and the President -- not with the Supreme Court.
